q: Bales left to oxidise in an attic for three years, at a price no pale ale brewer would pay for fresh ones, are exactly what a Brussels lambic house orders. What is that hop charge for?
opts: The cheesy, oxidised note that defines the finished beer's aroma
Colour, drawn from the browned leaf during the long boil
A bargain source of bittering, since drying concentrates the alpha acids
Preservation, with bitterness and aroma deliberately faded away
exp: A wort that will spend years fermenting needs the antiseptic side of the hop without its flavour, so lambic brewers hop heavily with bales whose alpha acids and oils have decayed to almost nothing. Fresh aromatic hops would fight the character the wild fermentation is meant to build, and their bitterness would sit badly in a beer this acidic.

q: Flour-cloudy wort, rich in raw starch and unfermentable dextrin, is exactly what a lambic brewhouse wants: rations for years of slow wild fermentation. Which mashing regime produces it?
exp: Milky, starchy liquid is pulled off early in the mash and the grist leans on a large share of unmalted wheat, leaving material a clean single-strain fermentation could never use. The organisms that arrive over the following years in the barrel can, and the regime remains standard practice in every traditional lambic brewhouse.

q: One word, protected across the EU as a traditional guarantee, sits in front of Geuze or Lambik on serious lists and separates the old-method article from its sweetened, filtered namesakes. Which word?
exp: Oude, vieille on French-language labels, is the traditional speciality guaranteed designation, and it requires the old method throughout: wholly spontaneous fermentation, real age in wood behind the bottle, and none of the sweetening and pasteurising the industrial versions lean on. On a list it is the single most reliable word for telling the sharp, cellarable article from the soda-sweet bottle at the same shelf height.

q: Sharps, sweets, bittersharps and bittersweets: the traditional Long Ashton scheme files every cider apple into one of four classes. Which two juice measurements draw the boundaries?
opts: Acidity and tannin
Pectin and nitrogen
Sugar and total acidity
Sugar and tannin
exp: The thresholds sit near two grams a litre of tannin and four and a half of malic acid, and the two lines cut the fruit into four quadrants. Sugar hardly separates cider fruit at all, since nearly everything grown for the press ferments fully; what a blender is balancing is bite against structure.

q: Low in malic acid and heavy in tannin, fruit of one class is the backbone of the classic West Country and Norman blends, giving a structure no dessert apple can. Which class is it?
exp: Bittersharps carry the same tannin with high acid on top, sharps bring acid alone, and sweets bring neither, so the bittersweet quadrant is the only one that gives body and grip without turning the blend austere. Dabinett and Yarlington Mill are the varieties an orchardist would name first.

q: Even when every fermentable sugar is gone, a perry keeps a gentle sweetness, because pear juice carries a sugar alcohol that yeast cannot touch. Name it.
exp: Sorbitol passes through fermentation untouched, so it survives into the driest perry as softness on the finish, along with the mildly laxative reputation older drinkers joke about. Pears also carry more citric acid than apples do, which is why a perry can taste brighter than a cider even while it finishes rounder.

q: Weeks pass in a Norman cider house while a brown pectin cap rises on the juice, the clear middle drawn off beneath it so starved of nutrients that the ferment crawls and stops sweet on its own. Name the technique.
exp: Pectin sets into a gel that floats off with most of the yeast nutrients, and the cidermaker racks the clean juice from under the chapeau brun. A fermentation that cannot finish is the whole point: the sweetness of a traditional cidre doux is kept by starvation rather than by filtration, pasteurisation or anything added.

q: Held at arm's length overhead, the bottle in an Asturian sidreria is crashed in a thin stream against the lip of a wide glass below, one short culin at a time, drunk off at once. Name that pour.
exp: The long drop knocks carbon dioxide briefly out of solution, so a still, sharp sidra natural reaches the mouth with a fleeting sparkle it never had in the bottle. Pouring only a swallow at a time follows from the same physics, since the lift is gone within moments and the glass is meant to be emptied before it fades.

q: Winter cold, not machinery, does the concentrating for most of Quebec's cidre de glace: autumn-pressed juice stands outdoors until the water locks up as ice and a dense syrup is drawn from beneath. Name that method.
exp: Concentrating the juice before fermentation is what lets ice cider reach its weight of sugar and acid in a climate built for the job. The rarer route presses whole apples left hanging frozen on the tree, and Quebec's rules recognise both while insisting the cold be the winter's own rather than a freezer's.

q: Twelve degrees Celsius shows on the cellar thermometer, and a guest has just sent back a handpulled best bitter as too warm. What should the director's note to the floor team say?
opts: Apologise and take cask beer off the list for the summer months
Fit an in-line chiller so every pint reaches the glass at four degrees
The cellar is right: cask bitter is meant for eleven to thirteen degrees
Move the casks to the four-degree cold room with the lagers overnight
exp: Cellar temperature is the style's specification rather than a refrigeration failure: at eleven to thirteen degrees the low carbonation and the malt read as intended, while colder service mutes the beer and at lager temperature it tastes flat and empty. The guest-facing answer is a word of explanation and an offered alternative, not chilling a living beer into silence.

q: Wide at the rim, usually stemmed, often printed with an abbey crest: one glass shape anchors the service standard for Trappist and abbey ales. Name the shape.
exp: A wide mouth lets the dense head settle to a thin cap and lifts the yeast and spice aromatics to the nose, and the open bowl gives a nine percent beer room to warm and unfold as it sits. The stem keeps the hand off the bowl, for the same reason it does on a wine glass: these are beers served closer to cellar than to fridge.

q: Brokers working for the 1855 exposition wrote down estate names, not plots of ground. What follows for a classified growth that later buys a neighbouring parcel?
opts: The estate drops a tier until the list is next reviewed
The parcel keeps the rank of whoever farmed it in 1855
Fruit from the added land is barred from the classified wine for fifty years after the purchase date
Fruit from the added land may go into the classified wine if that land holds the appellation
exp: This is the standing complaint against 1855: it ranked commercial names rather than delimited vineyard, so holdings could grow, shrink and swap without the rank moving. The rank travels with the name, and the new parcel has to be inside the appellation the classified wine is sold under before its fruit can go in. A Burgundian classification does the opposite, fixing the boundary and letting the owner change.

q: A guest insists the red side of the 1855 ranking has never been altered. Which correction is accurate?
opts: It is rebuilt every decade in the same way Saint-Emilion's is
It has been altered twice, and the second time was in 1973
It has been altered once, when Haut-Brion was written in during 1953
It has been altered three times, the last of them in the 1990s
exp: Cantemerle was omitted and inserted within a year of publication, and Mouton Rothschild rose from Second to First in 1973. Those are the only two changes of rank; the rest of the movement on the list has been estates dividing, which is how the 58 chateaux of 1855 became the 61 recognised now. Haut-Brion was in the original list from the start, which is what makes that distractor tempting to anyone who half-remembers the Graves connection.

q: Left off the exposition list and restored as a Fifth Growth within the year after its owner objected, which Medoc estate was the first correction ever made?
accept: chateau cantemerle in the haut medoc
exp: The wine had been sold direct to the Dutch trade rather than through the Bordeaux market, so the brokers had no local price record for it. That is a neat illustration of what the list was really measuring: presence on one city's exchange.

q: Below Chateau d'Yquem, the Sauternes side of 1855 holds two ranks of classified growth. Name them.
accept: premier cru classe and deuxieme cru classe
deuxieme cru classe and premier cru classe
premier cru classe deuxieme cru classe
premiers crus classes and deuxiemes crus classes
exp: Yquem sits alone above them as Premier Cru Superieur, a tier invented for it. The reds got five tiers and the sweet wines two, which tells you how much finer the price gradations were thought to be on the Left Bank.

q: Suppose a classified chateau buys vineyard from an unclassified neighbour. Which national body decides whether that ground is entitled to the appellation the classified wine carries?
accept: institut national de l'origine et de la qualite
exp: The rank is a private nineteenth-century verdict, but the appellation on the same label is a state matter, and parcel eligibility is settled by the INAO against the delimited zone. So the classification cannot be enlarged by purchase alone: the land has to already be inside the right appellation.
